title: Bodiless among bodies
theme: Knowing the self as bodiless among bodies, steady among the unsteady, great and all-pervading, the wise one does not grieve.

sandhi.rule: Final m → anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).
u before a dissimilar vowel becomes v, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).
Final m → anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः); final m stays before a vowel.
aḥ → o before n, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च).

sandhi_exceptions.note: śarīreṣu anavastheṣu: final u before a is not joined; the vishvAsa mūla and Madhva’s text join it (śarīreṣv anavastheṣv, corrections.json, orthographic), and Śaṅkara’s lemma keeps it apart as the base does. The unjoined u keeps the first pāda at eight syllables.

samasa.meaning: in those that have no stability

morphology.note: Absolutive of man ‘think’: ‘having known, having recognised’; Śaṅkara supplies the content, ‘I am this’.
From an- + avasthā ‘standing firm’; as the last member of a bahuvrīhi the final ā is shortened (anavastha).
‘Bodiless’, set against शरीरेषु: the self abides in bodies without being one.

translation.literal: ‘Having known the self, bodiless among bodies, abiding among the unstable, great, all-pervading, the wise one does not grieve.’
translation.readable: ‘The wise, who know the self — without a body among bodies, steady among things that never stay, vast and everywhere — do not grieve.’

anvaya: धीरः अनवस्थेषु शरीरेषु अवस्थितम् अशरीरम् महान्तम् विभुम् आत्मानम् मत्वा न शोचति ॥
syntax: One sentence. The first line and महान्तं विभुम् are accusative qualifiers of ātmānam, the object of the absolutive matvā; the main clause is dhīro na śocati. The line sets pairs against each other: aśarīram / śarīreṣu, anavastheṣu / avasthitam.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the one self, in its own nature like space, «स्वेन रूपेणाकाशकल्प आत्मा»; the word ātman is used to show it is not other than one’s own self, «आत्मग्रहणं स्वतोऽनन्यत्वप्रदर्शनार्थम्». Raṅgarāmānuja: without a body made by karma, «कर्मकृतशरीररहितम्», continuing his reading of 1.2.20–21 as the Supreme.
Śaṅkara: vibhu answers the doubt that ‘great’ might be relative: it means pervading, «विभुं व्यापिनम्». Raṅgarāmānuja takes the pair together as ‘possessed of great glory’, «महावैभवशालिनं».

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Counted as written, 16 and 16 syllables; written with the sandhi of the other witnesses, the first pāda would have seven.

beginner: This verse gives the reason why knowing the self ends grief. Bodies come and go; none of them stays. But the self that lives in them has no body of its own, stays steady, and is vast and present everywhere. A wise person who has understood this does not grieve. Śaṅkara says the self is like space: it is inside every body without being one. He adds that the verse says 'self' on purpose, to remind us that this is not something far away but our own self. Raṅgarāmānuja reads the verse as speaking of the supreme Lord, who has no body made by past actions. Either way the point is practical: grief clings to what changes, and the verse points the mind to what does not.
analogy: Like a river’s name: the water in it is never the same from one day to the next, yet it is the same river.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That the wise one who knows the self — bodiless among bodies, steady among the unstable, great and pervading — does not grieve.

commentary.q: Why does such knowledge end grief?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: grief has no ground in one who knows the self as this: «न ह्येवंविधस्वात्मविदः शोकोपपत्तिः». The bodies of gods, ancestors and men are impermanent; the self in them is eternal and unchanging, «अवस्थितं नित्यम् अविकृतमित्येतत्».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Briefly: bodiless means without a body made by karma, «कर्मकृतशरीररहितम्»; the self dwells in unstable bodies as their permanent element, and ‘great, pervading’ means possessed of great glory, «महावैभवशालिनं». The next verse, he says, gives the means of reaching such a self.

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: In our source Madhva gives this verse and the next two without comment; the bhāṣya resumes at 1.3.1. His mūla joins śarīreṣv anavastheṣv (corrections.json).

advaita.text: The self is one’s own self, like space in every body: «आत्मग्रहणं स्वतोऽनन्यत्वप्रदर्शनार्थम्». Knowing it as ‘I am this’ leaves no ground for grief.

visistadvaita.text: The Supreme dwells in bodies without a body made by karma, «कर्मकृतशरीररहितम्», and knowing him the wise do not grieve.

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara stresses that the bodiless self is one’s own; Raṅgarāmānuja that it is the Supreme, free of karma-made bodies. Madhva, in our source, does not comment.

parallels.note: The Gītā’s contrast of perishable bodies and the eternal embodied one.
The imperishable among the perishing — the same contrast as anavastheṣv avasthitam.

contemporary.text: Grief follows attachment to what changes, and almost everything changes. The verse does not forbid love of the changing; it asks whether anything in us stays, and whether knowing that could steady us. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: What in your life has stayed the same while everything around it changed?
reflect.deeper: Why does Śaṅkara insist that ‘ātman’ here means one’s own self and not something other?
reflect.practice: When you next feel loss, name what changed, and then name what in you is aware of the change.

flags.note: The vishvAsa mūla and Madhva’s text write śarīreṣv anavastheṣv avasthitam with the hiatus joined (corrections.json, orthographic).
